questions.question: In large-scale LLM training, what is the primary distinction between tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism?
questions.choice_A: Tensor parallelism splits individual layers’ computations (e.g., matrix multiplications) across devices, while pipeline parallelism partitions the model’s layers into sequential stages across devices.
questions.choice_B: Tensor parallelism partitions the dataset across devices, while pipeline parallelism duplicates the model across devices.
questions.choice_C: Tensor parallelism reduces communication by eliminating collectives, while pipeline parallelism focuses on overlapping communication with computation.
questions.choice_D: Tensor parallelism is only applicable to CNNs, while pipeline parallelism is only applicable to transformers.

questions.question: Which statement best describes sequence parallelism in the context of transformer training?
questions.choice_A: It replicates the entire model across all workers and averages gradients at the end of each step.
questions.choice_B: It shards activations and certain computations along the sequence length dimension to reduce per-device activation memory.
questions.choice_C: It moves attention layers to CPUs while keeping MLP layers on GPUs to save GPU memory.
questions.choice_D: It partitions tokens by vocabulary to improve embedding lookup throughput.

questions.question: In RL fine-tuning of LLMs (e.g., PPO), why might one prefer a separate value model rather than a shared actor-value head on the same backbone?
questions.choice_A: A separate value model always converges faster regardless of data regime.
questions.choice_B: A shared head cannot produce stable gradients in long-context settings.
questions.choice_C: A separate value model allows decoupled capacity and reduces interference between policy and value representations, at the cost of extra memory and compute.
questions.choice_D: A shared head is incompatible with mixed-precision training and gradient checkpointing.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of interleaved pipeline parallelism compared to naive pipeline parallelism?
questions.choice_A: It eliminates the need for microbatching entirely.
questions.choice_B: It makes tensor parallelism unnecessary for large models.
questions.choice_C: It reduces the memory footprint by removing activations from the pipeline.
questions.choice_D: It reduces pipeline bubbles by assigning multiple disjoint layer chunks per device to increase concurrency.

questions.question: When training with very long contexts, which batching strategy typically maximizes throughput without exceeding memory limits?
questions.choice_A: Token-based batching with a cap on total tokens per batch, combined with packing and minimal padding.
questions.choice_B: Fixed-number-of-sequences per batch regardless of length variability.
questions.choice_C: Sorting sequences randomly each step to avoid overfitting to length distributions.
questions.choice_D: Uniform padding to the global maximum length seen in the dataset.

questions.question: Which optimization most directly reduces activation memory without changing the model’s parameter count?
questions.choice_A: Using larger tensor parallelism degree.
questions.choice_B: Activation (gradient) checkpointing, which recomputes intermediates during the backward pass.
questions.choice_C: Switching from BF16 to FP16 precision.
questions.choice_D: Doubling the number of pipeline stages.

questions.question: In distributed training, what is a key practical difference between ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3-style optimizer sharding?
questions.choice_A: ZeRO-2 shards only the embeddings, while ZeRO-3 shards all residual connections.
questions.choice_B: ZeRO-2 shards gradients and optimizer states, while ZeRO-3 additionally shards model parameters themselves across data-parallel ranks.
questions.choice_C: ZeRO-2 eliminates all communication, while ZeRO-3 requires no checkpointing.
questions.choice_D: ZeRO-2 is incompatible with tensor parallelism, while ZeRO-3 requires CPU offloading.

questions.question: Which scenario most strongly motivates the use of FlashAttention or similar memory-efficient attention kernels?
questions.choice_A: Small batch sizes with short sequences where compute is dominant.
questions.choice_B: Models with minimal head count and shallow depth.
questions.choice_C: CPU-only training where GPU memory is not a constraint.
questions.choice_D: Long-context training where attention memory and bandwidth are bottlenecks, and IO-aware kernels can reduce reads/writes.

questions.question: In RL training of LLMs, which metric is most critical to monitor to avoid over-optimization against the reference behavior?
questions.choice_A: The KL divergence between the current policy and the reference model policy, often with a target range enforced via a penalty.
questions.choice_B: Only the supervised loss on the preference dataset.
questions.choice_C: GPU utilization percentage, independent of reward trends.
questions.choice_D: Number of parameters in the actor model.

questions.question: What is a practical advantage of Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) over classic data parallel when training very large models?
questions.choice_A: FSDP eliminates the need for any collectives during training.
questions.choice_B: FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across ranks, enabling fitting larger models in memory at the cost of more communication.
questions.choice_C: FSDP makes pipeline and tensor parallelism obsolete for trillion-parameter models.
questions.choice_D: FSDP requires no changes to checkpointing or initialization procedures.

questions.question: Which combination most effectively increases end-to-end tokens-per-second for a fixed hardware budget?
questions.choice_A: Using smaller batch sizes and disabling fused kernels.
questions.choice_B: Maximizing padding for consistent tensor shapes.
questions.choice_C: Overlapping communication with computation (e.g., gradient reduce-scatter overlap), using fused kernels, and tuning microbatch/accumulation to saturate hardware.
questions.choice_D: Forcing determinism by disabling kernel autotuning.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when evaluating at scale during RLHF training?
questions.choice_A: Running evaluations too frequently to detect regressions.
questions.choice_B: Using the same prompts across all evaluation runs to ensure reproducibility.
questions.choice_C: Collecting only reward-model scores without human-aligned metrics or reference-free measures like toxicity or truthfulness.
questions.choice_D: Logging too many metrics such as KL, entropy, and acceptance rates.

questions.question: For reproducibility in multi-parallel training (data, tensor, pipeline), which practice is most important?
questions.choice_A: Using a single global seed without regard to parallel group memberships.
questions.choice_B: Seeding per-parallelism group (e.g., data-parallel, tensor-parallel, pipeline stages), persisting RNG states, and controlling nondeterministic kernels when needed.
questions.choice_C: Relying on hardware ECC to ensure determinism.
questions.choice_D: Saving only model weights without optimizer states.

questions.question: What is the principal tradeoff when increasing pipeline depth to fit a larger model?
questions.choice_A: Reduced need for microbatching.
questions.choice_B: Increased pipeline bubbles and inter-stage communication, which can lower utilization unless microbatching/interleaving is tuned.
questions.choice_C: Guaranteed improvement in tokens-per-second due to better load balancing.
questions.choice_D: No impact on activation memory footprint.

questions.question: In PPO-style RLHF, which set of logged metrics best supports diagnosing optimization health?
questions.choice_A: Only total loss and step time.
questions.choice_B: Vocabulary size, parameter count, and FLOPs per token.
questions.choice_C: Policy loss, value loss, KL to reference, entropy, reward statistics (mean/variance), and episode lengths or completion rates.
questions.choice_D: BLEU and ROUGE exclusively.

questions.question: Why might BF16 be preferred over FP16 in large-scale mixed-precision training?
questions.choice_A: BF16 uses fewer bits than FP16, further reducing memory.
questions.choice_B: BF16 has a wider exponent range, reducing overflow/underflow issues while retaining performance benefits of 16-bit compute.
questions.choice_C: BF16 guarantees deterministic results across all hardware.
questions.choice_D: BF16 eliminates the need for loss scaling strategies entirely in all cases.

questions.question: What is a recommended practice for checkpointing very large sharded models to balance speed, reliability, and storage?
questions.choice_A: Save only the consolidated (gathered) weights to a single file to simplify recovery.
questions.choice_B: Disable optimizer state saving to cut storage in half.
questions.choice_C: Use partitioned (per-rank) checkpoints with versioned metadata, include optimizer and RNG states, and validate via checksums or manifest files.
questions.choice_D: Perform checkpoints only at the end of training to minimize I/O overhead.

questions.question: How does context window size impact training throughput and memory?
questions.choice_A: Longer contexts reduce memory due to fewer batches per step.
questions.choice_B: Throughput is unaffected; only accuracy changes.
questions.choice_C: Longer contexts increase activation memory and attention compute/bandwidth, often requiring reduced batch size or memory-efficient attention to maintain throughput.
questions.choice_D: Context window size only impacts inference, not training.

questions.question: In distributed RL training for LLMs, which strategy helps keep actor experience generation and learner updates synchronized without stalling?
questions.choice_A: Single-threaded rollout and update on a single GPU.
questions.choice_B: Asynchronous sampling with queues/buffers, off-policy correction if needed, and backpressure via rate-limiting on producers or consumers.
questions.choice_C: Dropping all trajectories that exceed a fixed length.
questions.choice_D: Only increasing the number of actors without changing the learner.

questions.question: Which communication pattern is most performance-critical for tensor-parallel transformer training on GPUs?
questions.choice_A: All-to-all for embedding lookups only.
questions.choice_B: Broadcast from rank 0 once per step.
questions.choice_C: Collectives such as all-reduce and reduce-scatter/all-gather within tensor-parallel groups, ideally overlapped with compute.
questions.choice_D: Point-to-point sends between random pairs of ranks.

questions.question: What is a practical way to detect and respond to regressions during large-scale evaluation of RL fine-tuning runs?
questions.choice_A: Rely solely on training reward to indicate progress.
questions.choice_B: Evaluate on a single static benchmark to simplify comparison.
questions.choice_C: Use a diverse, versioned eval suite with per-domain metrics, track confidence intervals over time, and gate deployments on statistically meaningful changes.
questions.choice_D: Only compare models by parameter count and FLOPs.
